title: Bowing, Shoes Off, and Soju Manners: A Beginner's Guide to Korean Etiquette
html:
Korean etiquette isn't a long list of strict rules you have to memorize before you land — it's mostly a handful of everyday habits that locals grow up with. This guide covers the etiquette that trips up first-time visitors the most: when to take your shoes off, how people greet each other, the small rules around drinking soju with others, and a few basic phrases that go a long way even if you don't speak any Korean.

Take Your Shoes Off Indoors

In Korea, homes almost always have a small raised entryway called a hyeon-gwan (홞관) right by the front door. This is where you take your shoes off before stepping up onto the main floor — the floor level itself usually changes slightly, so it's easy to spot even if nobody says anything. The same rule applies at most traditional restaurants with low tables and floor seating, at temples, and at hanok guesthouses (traditional Korean houses that now often work as small hotels).

You usually don't need to take your shoes off at cafes, casual restaurants with regular chairs and tables, convenience stores, or shops — if you're not sure, just glance at the entrance. A shoe rack, a pile of shoes by the door, or slippers laid out are all clear signs to take yours off too.

What locals actually do: even in modern apartments with regular flooring, almost every Korean household still keeps a shoe rack right by the door and switches to slippers or bare feet once inside. Walking in with your shoes on, even just to grab something quickly, is one of the fastest ways to make a Korean host wince.

Traditional Korean rooms like this are meant to be walked on in socks or bare feet, not shoes. Photo: Adbar, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0. Source.

How Koreans Greet Each Other: Bowing, Names, and Basic Phrases

The standard Korean greeting is a small bow — just a quick nod forward from the shoulders, not a deep formal bend. Men often add a handshake on top of the bow in business settings, but a bow on its own is completely normal everywhere else. When you hand someone something important, like a business card, a gift, or money, it's polite to use both hands (or your right hand supported lightly by your left) rather than just tossing it over with one hand.

A few phrases will take you a long way: annyeonghaseyo (안녕하세요) means "hello," and gamsahamnida (검사합니다) means "thank you." Both are polite, formal-enough versions that work in almost any situation as a tourist, from a taxi driver to a shop clerk.

What locals actually do: Koreans bow shallowly to almost everyone throughout the day — a shopkeeper, a bus driver, a coworker passing in the hallway. It's quick and casual, not a formal ceremony, so don't overthink it. A small nod of the head while saying annyeonghaseyo covers most everyday situations just fine.

One more small courtesy: near popular photo spots like Gyeongbokgung Palace, you'll often see people (tourists and locals alike) wearing rented hanbok, Korea's traditional dress. If you'd like a photo with someone dressed like this, ask first instead of snapping a candid shot — the same courtesy you'd expect back home.

Renting a hanbok for a day and taking photos at a palace or historic site is a popular, low-cost activity — just ask before photographing strangers wearing one. Photo via Wikimedia Commons (Wiki Loves Folklore 2023, South Korea), CC BY-SA 4.0. Source.

Soju and Drinking Etiquette: Pour for Others, Not Yourself

Soju is Korea's most common distilled spirit, usually shared at a table over food. There's one rule that surprises a lot of visitors: you're not supposed to pour your own glass. Instead, you fill the glass of the person next to you, and they fill yours. When you're pouring for someone older or more senior than you, it's polite to hold the bottle with your right hand and support your right wrist lightly with your left hand.

If you're drinking with someone noticeably older, you may notice younger people turning their head slightly to the side when they actually drink, as a small sign of respect. This custom is more relaxed among friends and younger coworkers today, but it's still common enough that it's worth knowing.

What locals actually do: at a shared table, Koreans keep half an eye on everyone's glass and top it off as soon as it gets low — so you may find your glass refilled often even if you never asked. That's just normal hospitality, not pressure to keep drinking. It's completely fine to leave your glass mostly full, switch to a soft drink, or say you don't drink at all — nobody will push you on it.

Soju is almost always poured for someone else, not for yourself. Photo: Charles Haynes, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0. Source.

Quick Reference: Basic Korean Phrases for Travelers

You don't need to be fluent — even mispronounced attempts at these get a warm reaction from most locals.

Korean How to say it What it means
안녕하세요 annyeonghaseyo Hello
검사합니다 gamsahamnida Thank you
윸셂합니다 joesonghamnida Sorry / excuse me
꿬 / 아니요 ne / aniyo Yes / no
이홄 주세요 igeo juseyo "This one, please" (while pointing)
업물예요? eolmayeyo? How much is it?
화장산이 어디예요? hwajangsili eodiyeyo? Where's the restroom?

💬 Got a Korean etiquette question we didn't cover here, like gift-giving or chopstick manners? Drop it in the comments below — happy to help you figure it out!
meta_description: A beginner's guide to Korean etiquette: when to take off shoes, how to bow and greet people, soju drinking manners, and key phrases every traveler should know.
